Of course, you have to add value. You need the skill yourself and enough authority that people trust you, or nobody buys it. If you've got that, look for people who already have a budget. Hobbyists are the first group. A knitter already spends money on yarn every month, so a $6 pattern barely registers. People building a skill come next. Someone learning guitar is already paying for lessons and strings, and they'll pay for the practice drills that get them there faster. The third group has a goal with a deadline, like a licensing exam or a first marathon. They're searching hard right now because the date is coming. Your job is to get a slice of money that's already being spent.

Your digital product checkout is more than a payment button. 👀 If you sell ebooks, templates, courses, guides, Canva templates, or other digital products, you need to think about what happens after someone clicks “buy.” Before selling your first digital product, make sure you have: 1️⃣ Purchase terms — what the customer is actually agreeing to when they buy. 2️⃣ License & use restrictions — what they can and cannot do with your product. 3️⃣ Privacy Policy — especially if you’re collecting customer information. 4️⃣ Website/store terms — the rules governing purchases and use of your store. 5️⃣ Protection against unauthorized sharing & reselling — because your digital product should not become the internet’s free download. 😭 Your creativity is an asset. Treat it like one. And remember: your legal protection shouldn’t start after someone steals or misuses your digital product. It should be part of your business from the beginning. Please let me save you from the “what digital product should I make?” spiral😂 Because I think beginners often start in the wrong place. They open Canva. They scroll through templates. They look at what everyone else is selling. And then wonder why they still have no idea what to create. Instead, start with the problem. What does the person you want to help keep struggling with? What are they trying to figure out? What would save them time, make something easier or help them get closer to a result? Then ask: “Could I turn the solution into something they can use?” That could become a: → guide → workbook → checklist → planner → tracker → template → resource You don’t need to invent something completely revolutionary. You need to create something useful to a specific person. And honestly?
